catalyst.body:
Feedback - Friction - Exposure

Feedback is by far the most common catalysts we bump into day to day professionally, and they come from two sources:

catalyst-collision.body: Creativity looks messy, but it isn't. catalysts are the spark that kicks off creative work. The more of these catalysts you have available.

catalyst-collision-exposure.body:
The more reactions you will have. 

You cannot control how or when all of the information combines, and sparks creativity, but you can understand why it happens and give yourself more opportunities to experience it.

catalyst-outcomes-exposure.body:
Exposure is not a direct catalyst like the two categories we have already covered. It's fuel. It's raw material. When you see novel solutions. Solutions that make you stop and say…how did they even come up with that. That is because of this.

Exposure gives you patterns to borrow. New metaphors. New possibilities.

catalyst-outcomes-feedback.body:
So, feedback gives us evidence. It tells us explicitly "here is what happened"

Friction is when reality does not match expectation. Friction says “Something is off” and it is up to you to notice it.

catalyst-outcomes-friction.body:
Feedback gives you evidence. It tells you what happened. 

Friction gives you direction. It tells you when something feels off. Your job is to do the work of figuring out what that is.

Exposure gives you possibility.

conclusion-worth-building.body:

exposure-practice-beaten-path.body:
In case it isn't obvious. Get off the beaten path. You will never unlock new possibilities, novel or unique solutions if the only stay in your lane.

Podcasts, other programming languages, other software discipline. Are easier ways to still stick in the general vicinity of making software and broaden your lens into what is possible, but I think you should go crazy. Try things that feel completely unrelated. Our brains are capable of making connections we could never predict if we just give it the raw material to work with.

feedback-complete.body:
The reason it is the most common catalyst is that feedback is explicit and already in context. It comes directly from the source and tells you exactly what is going on.

Most of the work that you end up doing is triggered by this type of catalyst. There are a few things to keep in mind though to make these catalysts more impactful.

feedback-practice.body:
This is a big one. All the feedback in the world means nothing if you do not see it.

There are a ton of ways to do this. I am not going to prescribe any, but I will share one of the newer ways that this is being done with AI at our fingertips.

feedback-practice-glass.body: Ramp has created an internal product called Glass. They have written a lot about this, but the gist is that it is a workspace for every employee that is already connected to everything. User metrics, product usage data, support tickets, internal comms, with AI tooling built in that allows every employee to have feedback at their fingertips no matter what they are working on.

feedback-practice-source.body:
The biggest mistake I see when using feedback as a catalyst is using the feedback as the source of what should happen. Feedback should always be treated as a signal, not the source.

Our job. The creative work that comes next is where that signal leads us. How we use that signal to find the right solutions.

Dax had a really good tweet that captured how this can look like in practice some times.

final-path-catalysts.body: It usually isn't one catalyst it is multiple.

final-path-ideas.body: Those catalysts don't generate a single idea. It is multiple. Sometimes they work together sometimes you follow them down their own path.

final-path-reality.body: But not every idea is good. Some are dead ends when you try to bring them into reality.

final-path-taste.body:
And the clarity you get exploring those ideas narrows the field further and you have to decide if what you have landed on is good enough, or you need to loop back and keep iterating.

Creativity is hard, but there is a rhythm. You expand. You contract. You riff. You refine.

friction.body:
These are the most familiar cases of friction. They are easier to evaluate because they are visible. You notice them and you can point directly to them.

But there are other types of friction as well.

friction-complex.body: These are complex cases of friction. I'm not going to say whether these are more valuable than the other kind of friction, but complex friction is hidden misalignment, and often these are the issues that make you pull your hair out trying to figure out why something isn't working or why users are behaving a certain way.

friction-practice-aperture.body: Zoom out on the point of friction.

friction-practice-aperture-expanded.body: Take a look at the bigger picture.

friction-practice-aperture-focus.body: Zoom in. Dive into the details and answer why this is needed?

friction-practice-aperture-network.body:
Take a look at what happened before. What happens after?

The more information you consume during the phase of creativity the higher the ceiling will be on the solutions you can produce during the steps that come next.

friction-practice-aperture-prompt.body: When friction rears it's head another technique you can use is changing your aperture.

friction-practice-ask-why.body:
When the cost of writing, and refactoring code is 0 what is the incentive to write smaller functions? Does it still exist? Maybe it does in some cases maybe it goes away entirely...the point is that we should pause and ask why did this matter and will it continue to matter moving forward?

The creative work this creates is the answer to "the old way doesn't make sense...what now?"

friction-practice-prompt.body: The best thing you can do when you run into, or observe friction is pause and ask why. You may recognize these knuckleheads. They are talking about a perfect example of how AI has changed an incentive based point of friction that has been a part of engineering best practice for decades.

There is a great book called the Mom Test that if you haven't heard about it yet you should go check it out, but it perfectly captures the truth about human psychology. 

As soon as someone starts talking to someone there is drift from reality.

less-sacred-constraints.body:
Sometimes it isn't getting started that is tough. It is getting past a dead end. Artificial Contraints are exactly what they sound like.

"What if I could only use one color", "What if I we only used a single API endpoint?"

Forced connections is the same goal but instead of limiting what is possible, you are forcing together two unrelated ideas and seeing what shakes out.

"What if API responses worked like GPS directions?"

"What if search worked like a public library?"

What these exercises produce don't have to be used, but they can shake things up and get you out of a creative rut.

less-sacred-eight-patterns.body:
There is a design exercise used when starting a new project.  You have to come up with 8 completely unrelated ideas in 8 minutes.

The goal of this exercise is to push past your first, most obvious idea, silence the ciritic in your head that says "nope thats not good" to get ideas on paper.

The best part about this approach is that you don't have to have a team or do this on you own anymore.

less-sacred-gangprompt.body: Finally this one. There is a reason pair programming has been a thing in our industry for decades, and this is the next iteration. Working on a single agent session together, with others.

less-sacred-paper.body: Paper, is a canvas based design tool.

less-sacred-paper-video.body: And they have this built into their product. Pull from real data sources, and design guidelines and get your agent to generate as many ideas as you want.

less-sacred-quick-video.body: The final tip is don't do it alone. This is Quick. A tool built by shopify so that anyone could share what they are working on.

less-sacred-smith-diction.body: Smith & Diction is one of my favorite brand studios. When they get a client EVERYONE works on the client in the same file. This let's everyone be inspired by each others work. Even if they aren't in the same room.

You know the right answer, not through a single moment of magic but because you found enough wrong answers to recognize the right one when it showed up.

Taste is when you have done this process so many times you’ve built intuition and you can find shortcuts to the finish line.

Which means, the way you get better at finding the right answer is by doing more.

We are looking at the path instead of the process.

Every creative path is messy when you trace it step by step. It bends. It doubles back. It wanders into places that do not make sense until later.

And if you compare one person’s path to another’s, they almost never match.

reality-practice-output-artifacts.body:
If there is one lesson you get about creativity from my entire talk it is this.

The output of creativity is not the artifacts you make along the way. The output is the understanding you gained while making them.

Artifacts are not precious. They are not special. They are a tool. A means to an end.

When you make something real, you create new catalysts. You give yourself something else to notice, and a way to continue the loop.

Artifacts are about getting clarity.

Because the goal isn’t perfection it is clarity.

shorten-the-loop.body:
The last thing we are going to cover today. This is this is the most common place that people get tripped up with creative work. You get over the hurdle of the “blank canvas” and get started, but then you try to solve the whole world. All at one time.

When you try to solve everything, you end up solving nothing

It’s overwhelming. It’s too much to solve at once. So either you give up, or you get lost. You spend too much time in the woods and never get to a high quality solution.

taste-pattern-matching.body:
Taste is pattern matching earned through pain.

We have been over this. Creativity isn’t magic. Neither is “taste”.

You know, there was this story I always heard as a kid, and when I heard it I remember it blowing my mind. It was about the people who worked for the government or banks whose job it was to detect counterfeit bills and they didn't use a special machine, they didn't use one of those markers. They could just touch a bill and know. It felt off. 

They had touched soooo many bills that they could immediately tell the difference between what was real and what was fake.
